theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go. The G-codes and M-codes in this test are those used on most machines; your machine's manual has the final say.

essays.stem: Explain the X, Y and Z axes of a CNC machine, and the difference between machine home and work zero.
essays.modelAnswer: A CNC machine moves its tool or torch along straight axes. On a plasma table or a vertical mill, X is usually the long left-to-right direction, Y is the front-to-back direction, and Z is up and down, along the spindle or torch. Plus Z moves the tool up and away from the work. Machine home, or machine zero, is a fixed point set by the maker. The machine finds it with its home switches when it is switched on, so it knows where its slides are. It does not change from job to job. Work zero is a point the operator chooses on the part or plate, such as its bottom-left corner or top surface, and all the positions in the program are measured from it. It is set for each job by moving the tool to that point and storing it as the work offset, so the program cuts in the right place on the plate.
markingPoints: X and Y across the table, Z along the spindle or torch
+Z moves the tool away from the work
Machine home is fixed by the maker and found by the home switches
Work zero is chosen on the part; program positions are measured from it
Work zero is set for each job (work offset)

essays.stem: Compare absolute (G90) and incremental (G91) programming. Use an example to show the difference.
essays.modelAnswer: In absolute programming (G90), every X, Y and Z value is measured from the work zero. In incremental programming (G91), every value is measured from where the tool is now, so it says how far to move, not where to go. Example: three holes are on a line at X20, X50 and X80, all at Y30. In absolute mode the program says X20 Y30, then X50 Y30, then X80 Y30. In incremental mode, after going to the first hole, it says X30 Y0, then X30 Y0, because each hole is 30 mm further on. Absolute programming is easier to check against a drawing dimensioned from one datum, and one mistake does not carry on to the following moves. Incremental is handy for repeated patterns, but a mistake in one move shifts every move after it. Most beginners write in absolute and switch to incremental only where it helps.
markingPoints: G90 measures every position from the work zero
G91 measures each move from the current position
A correct worked example in both modes
Absolute is easier to check and errors do not build up
Incremental is useful for repeated patterns but errors carry on

essays.stem: Explain what G00, G01, G02 and G03 do, and when each one is used in a program.
essays.modelAnswer: G00 is a rapid move. The machine moves as fast as it can to a new position, not cutting, and the path may not be a straight line. It is used to move to the start of a cut or away from the part, and must only be used where the tool is clear of the work and any clamps. G01 is a straight-line move at the feed rate set by the F word. It is used for cutting straight edges, slots and sides of a part. G02 cuts an arc in a clockwise direction at the feed rate, and G03 cuts an arc anticlockwise. For both, the program gives the end point and either the radius with R or the centre with I and J. They are used for round corners, holes and curved edges. On a plasma table, the arc must be cut in the right direction so the kerf falls on the scrap side.
markingPoints: G00 rapid, non-cutting move to position, only where clear of the work
G01 straight cutting move at the feed rate F
G02 clockwise arc; G03 anticlockwise arc
Arcs need the end point and R or I and J
Sensible example of use for each

essays.stem: Write a short program to cut a 100 mm × 50 mm rectangle on a CNC plasma table, with work zero at the bottom-left corner, and explain each line.
essays.modelAnswer: (RECTANGLE 100 X 50) is a comment that names the job. G21 G90 sets millimetres and absolute mode. G00 X0 Y0 makes a rapid move to the bottom-left corner, the work zero. M03 switches the torch on; many plasma controls use M03 and M05 for the torch, but the machine manual must be checked. G01 X100 Y0 F2000 cuts along the bottom edge at a feed of 2000 mm per minute, or the feed the cut chart gives for the plate. G01 X100 Y50 cuts up the right side. G01 X0 Y50 cuts along the top. G01 X0 Y0 cuts down the left side back to the start. M05 switches the torch off. G00 X0 Y0 is a safe move home, and M30 ends the program and rewinds it. In real work I would add a lead-in in the scrap and kerf compensation so the part is cut to size.
markingPoints: Sets units and absolute mode (G21 G90)
Rapid to start, torch on (M03 or the machine's code)
Four correct G01 moves with a feed rate
Torch off and program end (M05, M30)
Explains each line; mentions lead-in or kerf compensation

essays.stem: Describe the steps to set up and run a new program safely on a CNC machine at the Centre.
essays.modelAnswer: First check the program on the computer with the simulation, comparing the shape and sizes with the drawing. Load it into the control and check that it is the right file. Home the machine. Clamp or place the plate or part firmly, square to the axes, and clear the table of tools and off-cuts. Set the work zero on the part and enter any tool or torch offsets. Check that all guards and screens are in place, the extraction or water table is working and the emergency stop works. Then do a dry run with the torch or spindle off, or well above the work, in single block mode at a low feed override, watching that every move is where it should be. The assessor checks the set-up before the machine cuts. Run the first cut at a low override, with your hand near the emergency stop, and stay at the machine. Check the first part against the drawing.
markingPoints: Checks the program by simulation against the drawing; loads the right file
Homes the machine, holds the work firmly, clears the table
Sets work zero and offsets; guards, extraction and e-stop checked
Dry run in single block at low override
Assessor checks set-up; first run supervised with hand near e-stop; first part checked

essays.stem: Explain how a part goes from a drawing to a cut part using CAD/CAM software and a CNC machine.
essays.modelAnswer: First the part is drawn to full size in CAD (computer-aided design) software, using the drawing's dimensions, and saved. The drawing is then opened in CAM (computer-aided manufacturing) software. Here the programmer chooses the material and thickness, the tool or the plasma cut settings, and the feed rate. The CAM software works out the toolpaths: where the tool or torch will go, with lead-ins, kerf compensation and the order of cuts, such as holes before the outside edge. Several parts can be nested on one plate to save steel. The toolpath is shown on screen and checked. Then a post-processor turns it into G-code written for that make of machine. The program file is saved with a clear name and sent to the machine by cable, network or memory stick. At the machine the operator sets up, sets work zero, dry runs and then cuts.
markingPoints: Part drawn in CAD to drawing sizes
CAM: material, tool/cut settings and feeds chosen; toolpaths made
Lead-ins, kerf compensation, cut order or nesting mentioned
Post-processor turns toolpath into machine-specific G-code
File saved and sent to the machine; set-up and dry run before cutting

essays.stem: Explain kerf, kerf compensation and lead-ins, and why holes are cut before the outside edge of a part on a CNC plasma table.
essays.modelAnswer: Kerf is the width of metal removed by the cut. If the torch ran along the line on the drawing, half the kerf would come off the part, so the part would be too small and the holes too large. Kerf compensation moves the torch path half a kerf width to the scrap side: outside the line for the outside edge, and inside the line for holes. It is set in the CAM software or with the control's compensation codes. A lead-in is a short cut that starts in the scrap and runs onto the part line. The arc pierces the plate in the scrap, where it leaves a rough mark, and then joins the line smoothly, so the finished edge is clean. A lead-out does the same at the end. Holes are cut first while the part is still held by the plate around it; if the outside were cut first, the part could move or tip and the holes would be in the wrong place.
markingPoints: Kerf is the width of the cut
Without compensation, parts are too small and holes too big
Compensation moves the path half a kerf to the scrap side
Lead-in puts the pierce in the scrap for a clean edge
Holes first, so the part does not move before they are cut

essays.stem: Describe the safety rules to follow when working with CNC cutting and machining equipment.
essays.modelAnswer: Only use a CNC machine after training and with the instructor's permission. Keep all guards, doors and screens in place, and never bypass a guard or interlock. Know where the emergency stop is and check that it works. The assessor checks the set-up before the machine runs. Keep hands, tools and loose clothing clear of moving parts while the program runs, and stay at the machine. Do not wear gloves, rings or loose sleeves near a rotating spindle or chuck, and tie back long hair. Wear safety glasses and safety boots. For plasma cutting, use a filter lens of the shade the maker gives, keep the extraction or water table working because of fumes, and treat cut parts and slag as hot. Stop the machine and isolate it before clearing chips, changing tools or reaching in. Report any fault at once.
markingPoints: Trained and permitted; guards and interlocks kept in place and never bypassed
Emergency stop known and checked; assessor checks the set-up
Hands and clothing clear; no gloves, rings or loose sleeves near rotating parts
PPE, plasma eye protection, fume extraction and hot parts
Stop and isolate before reaching in; report faults

essays.stem: Explain how you would find and correct mistakes in a new CNC program before it cuts a part.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the program through line by line against the drawing. Check that it has the right units (G21 for mm) and mode (G90 or G91), that each X and Y value matches a point on the drawing measured from the work zero, and that the signs (plus or minus) are right. Check that the torch or spindle is switched on before cutting moves and off at the end, and that there is a feed rate. Then run a graphic simulation on the computer or the control and compare the shape with the drawing; mistakes such as a wrong number, a missing line or an arc in the wrong direction show up clearly. If the control gives an alarm, read the message and go to the line it names. At the machine, do a dry run in single block mode with the feed override low. Correct each mistake, save the program under a new version name and check it again.
markingPoints: Reads the program against the drawing: units, mode, coordinates, signs
Checks spindle or torch on/off codes and feed rate
Uses simulation to compare the toolpath with the drawing
Reads alarms and goes to the named line
Dry runs in single block; corrects and saves a new version

essays.stem: Explain why CNC programs must be clearly named, commented and stored, and what a set-up sheet should record.
essays.modelAnswer: A workshop may have hundreds of programs. A clear name, such as the part number, material and version, means the right program is loaded and an old or wrong one is not cut by mistake. Programs are kept in one set folder with a backup, so they are not lost if the computer or control fails, and a good program is not overwritten. Comments in brackets in the program tell the next person what each section does, such as which tool or which hole, so they can check or change it safely. When a program is changed, it is saved under a new version number and the change is noted. A set-up sheet goes with the program. It records the part name and drawing number, the material and thickness, where work zero is, how the work is held, the tools or torch settings, the feeds, and any special points. This lets anyone set up and run the job the same way next time.
markingPoints: Clear names stop the wrong program being run
Stored in a set folder with backups; not overwritten
Comments explain sections for the next person
Changes saved as new versions and noted
Set-up sheet: part, material, work zero, work holding, tools or cut settings, feeds

practical1.title: Write, plot and simulate a CNC program for a flat bracket
practical1.brief: As a group, write a CNC program by hand for a flat steel bracket from the instructor's drawing: a 120 mm × 80 mm plate with two 20 mm holes. Choose and mark the work zero on the drawing, then list the X and Y value of every point. Write the program in absolute mode with comments: units, mode, moves to each hole, the holes cut first (G02 or G03 full circles, or as the instructor directs), then the outside edge, the torch on and off codes your machine uses, and program end. Each member writes and explains one section of the program. Plot the toolpath on graph paper at full size or half size to check it. Then enter the program in the CNC simulation software on a Centre computer (or the machine's own simulator) and run it, comparing the shape with the drawing. Correct any errors and save the program with a clear name. This practical needs no CNC machine. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: The instructor's drawing of the bracket
Program sheets, graph paper, rule, compass and pencils
Computer with CNC simulation software (or the machine's simulator)
List of the G-codes and M-codes the Centre's machine uses
photos: The drawing with the work zero marked and the table of X and Y values
The toolpath plotted on graph paper
The program entered in the simulation software
The simulation running, showing the full toolpath
The corrected program saved, with its file name on screen
checklist: Chose a sensible work zero and listed correct X and Y values
Wrote a section of the program with correct G-codes, M-codes and feed
Cut the holes before the outside edge
Explained what each line of their section does
Plotted or checked the toolpath against the drawing
Found and corrected at least one error, or confirmed none, using the simulation
Saved the program with a clear name and version
safety: Sit correctly at the computer and take short breaks from the screen
Keep drinks away from computers and keyboards
Keep cables tidy so no one trips
Do not load any program to a machine without the assessor's say-so

practical2.title: Set up, dry run and cut a part on a CNC machine
practical2.brief: As a group, set up and run the program from Practical 1 on the Centre's CNC plasma table (or CNC router or mill, using a suitable material). Load the program and check it on the machine's graphics. Home the machine, place and hold the plate, and set the work zero on the plate. Check the guards, screens, extraction and emergency stop. Do a dry run with the torch or spindle off, in single block mode at low feed override. The assessor checks the set-up before the machine cuts anything. Then cut the part at a reduced override, with one member at the emergency stop. Let the part cool, then measure it against the drawing and record the sizes. Each member does one set-up step (loading, work zero, dry run, emergency stop watch, or measuring) and measures one dimension. If the Centre has no CNC machine, do the task in the simulation software instead: set up a virtual work zero, run the program in single block with screenshots at each step, and fill in a set-up sheet for a real machine, and say so on the record. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Program from Practical 1, checked and saved
CNC plasma table (or CNC router or mill) with its manual and cut chart
Steel plate about 3–6 mm thick, or material suited to the machine
Tape measure, steel rule and vernier caliper
Plasma eye protection of the maker's shade, safety glasses, boots, leather gloves for handling cut parts away from the machine
Set-up sheet; computer with simulation software (if there is no CNC machine)
photos: The program loaded and shown on the machine's graphics
The plate held on the table and the work zero being set
The guards, extraction and emergency stop checked
The dry run in single block with the torch or spindle off
The cut part, cooled, being measured against the drawing
The completed set-up sheet and the cleaned machine
checklist: Loaded the correct program and checked it on the graphics
Held the plate firmly and set the work zero correctly
Checked guards, extraction and the emergency stop before running
Did a dry run in single block at low override
Waited for the assessor's check before cutting
Stood clear of moving parts and wore the right PPE; no gloves near rotating parts
Measured the part and recorded the sizes against the drawing
Filled in the set-up sheet and cleaned the machine
safety: All guards and screens on; never bypass an interlock
The assessor checks the set-up before the machine runs; one member keeps a hand near the emergency stop
No gloves, rings or loose sleeves near rotating spindles; tie back long hair
For plasma: correct filter shade, extraction on, and treat cut parts and slag as hot
